findings.title: Race condition in BlockedEmail.should_block? read-modify-write of match_count
findings.body: should_block? loads the record, increments match_count in memory, and saves it. Two concurrent signup attempts with the same blocked email can both read match_count = 0, both write 1, losing one increment. More importantly, the save is a full-record UPDATE with no locking, so under concurrent load the statistics (match_count, last_match_at) can be silently lost. Use an atomic SQL update (e.g. BlockedEmail.where(email: email).update_all('match_count = match_count + 1, last_match_at = ?', Time.zone.now)) or lock the row, and re-read the action_type after the update.

findings.title: should_block? performs a write during validation, and its return value is wrong when no record exists
findings.body: BlockedEmail.should_block? is called from EmailValidator.validate_each (lib/validators/email_validator.rb:13), i.e. during User validation, yet it mutates the database (increments match_count, sets last_match_at, saves). This means a mere validation attempt — including failed validations, GET-triggered checks, or User.new(...).valid? in a console — permanently writes to blocked_emails. Also, when no record exists, `record` is nil and the method returns nil (falsy) — fine — but when a record exists with action_type :do_nothing, it still performs the write even though the email will not be blocked, inflating match_count for emails that are explicitly allowed. The statistics write should be moved out of the validation path (e.g. into the controller after a failed signup, or done atomically and only when actually blocking).

findings.title: Email matching is case-sensitive; blocked emails can be bypassed with case variation
findings.body: should_block? does `BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first` with no downcasing or normalization. The users table stores email as given (User validates uniqueness on the raw email string), and the signup form sends whatever the user typed. An attacker who adds a BlockedEmail entry for 'spam@example.com' can trivially bypass it by registering 'SPAM@example.com' or 'Spam@Example.com'. The lookup must normalize: `BlockedEmail.where(email: Email.downcase(email)).first` (the codebase already has Email.downcase used in users_controller.rb:269), and ideally the email column should be stored downcased on create (before_validation). Without this the entire blocklist feature is ineffective.

findings.title: Blocked-email check is skipped when the email is blank or nil
findings.body: validate_each receives `value` which is the raw attribute. If value is nil (email not yet assigned) or an empty string, `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)` is still called with nil/'' — for nil, `where(email: nil).first` returns nil so it is harmless, but the guard `record.errors[attribute].blank?` means the blocked check only runs when no other error exists. More importantly, the validator never checks that value is a syntactically valid email before doing the domain regex match: `value =~ regexp` on line 21 will raise NoMethodError (undefined method =~ for nil) if value is nil when a whitelist/blacklist setting is present, crashing validation with a 500 instead of a validation error. Add `return if value.blank?` at the top of validate_each.

findings.title: Domain whitelist/blacklist regex is injectable and matches substrings
findings.body: email_in_restriction_setting? builds a Regexp directly from the SiteSetting value: `Regexp.new("@(#{domains})", true)` after only escaping dots. The setting is admin-controlled so the injection risk is limited to admins, but the bigger correctness/security bug is that the pattern is unanchored: '@(example\.com)' matches 'user@sub.example.com' AND 'user@notexample.com' (substring match, no boundary). A blacklist entry for 'example.com' will also block 'myexample.com', and a whitelist entry for 'example.com' will wrongly admit 'user@evilexample.com'. The domain list should be split on commas/whitespace and each domain anchored: Regexp.new("@#{Regexp.escape(domain)}$", true) per domain, matching any of them. This is a real bypass/false-positive issue for the email restriction feature that this PR relocates into the validator.

findings.title: Changing email validation from separate presence/uniqueness validators to combined `validates` alters error messages and hash shape returned to the client
findings.body: The old code used `validates_presence_of :email` and `validates_uniqueness_of :email`, which add errors like 'Email can't be blank' and 'Email has already been taken'. The new `validates :email, presence: true, uniqueness: true` produces the same default messages, so that part is equivalent — but the PR also adds `errors: user.errors.to_hash` and `values: user.attributes.slice(...)` to the create failure response in users_controller.rb. The client (create_account_controller.js:274) checks `result.errors && result.errors.email` — with to_hash, errors.email is an array of message strings, which works — but the change from the previous response shape (message only) is an API contract change for any other API consumer, and `user.attributes.slice("name", "username", "email")` echoes back the submitted email verbatim, including any HTML/script content, into a JSON response that the client pushes into rejectedEmails and re-renders; ensure the client treats it as text (it does, via Ember binding) but note the response now includes raw user input. The bigger issue: uniqueness validation on email is not case-insensitive — 'User@Example.com' and 'user@example.com' are treated as different by `validates :uniqueness_of`, yet the DB unique index on users.email is also case-sensitive, so this is consistent, but the BlockedEmail lookup (see separate finding) is what must be case-insensitive.

findings.title: Error response now includes raw submitted attributes (name, username, email) without sanitization
findings.body: The create failure path now returns `values: user.attributes.slice("name", "username", "email")`. These are the raw, un-sanitized params the user submitted (set via User.new_from_params). The values are echoed back in the JSON response and the JS client pushes result.values.email into rejectedEmails and compares it against the email input. While Ember escapes on render, returning raw user input in an API response is an unnecessary reflection vector; at minimum the email should be the normalized/downcased form. Consider returning only what is needed (the email) and normalizing it.

findings.title: rejectedEmails comparison is case-sensitive, so a rejected email can be re-submitted with different casing
findings.body: The client-side check `this.get('rejectedEmails').contains(email)` compares the exact string. If the server rejected 'Spam@Example.com', the user can immediately retype 'spam@example.com' (or any case variation) and the client-side check passes; the form will be re-submitted and only fail again server-side. The comparison should be case-insensitive (compare downcased values), matching the server-side normalization the BlockedEmail lookup should have (see related finding). Also note the server returns the email in result.values.email — if the server normalizes differently than the client, the client-side rejection will never trigger.

findings.title: blocked_emails.email has no length limit and no normalization; unique index is case-sensitive
findings.body: t.string :email with no limit defaults to 255 in most adapters, but there is no downcasing on store and the unique index on email is case-sensitive (default PostgreSQL behavior). Combined with the case-sensitive lookup in BlockedEmail.should_block?, entries 'Spam@x.com' and 'spam@x.com' are treated as distinct rows, defeating the blocklist. The migration should either add a functional unique index on lower(email) or enforce downcasing in the model's before_validation, and the model should normalize on lookup.

findings.title: No test for case-insensitive matching of blocked emails
findings.body: The spec suite for BlockedEmail covers default action_type, statistics updates, and both action types, but never tests that should_block? matches an email regardless of case (e.g. record 'block@spam.org' vs query 'BLOCK@SPAM.ORG'). Given that email case-insensitivity is a real-world requirement (and the current implementation is case-sensitive, which is a bug), this is exactly the scenario that needs a regression test. Add a test asserting BlockedEmail.should_block?('BLOCK@SPAMFROMHOME.ORG') returns true when the stored record is lowercase.

findings.title: EmailValidator spec does not test the whitelist/blacklist domain logic that was moved into it
findings.body: The spec only stubs BlockedEmail.should_block? and checks the blocked path. The validator also contains the relocated email_domains_whitelist / email_domains_blacklist logic (lines 4-12), which is security-relevant (it is the only thing preventing signups from blacklisted domains). There are no tests covering: whitelist present and email not in whitelist → error; whitelist present and email in whitelist → no error; blacklist present and email in blacklist → error; blacklist present and email not in blacklist → no error. Since this PR moves that logic from User into EmailValidator, the existing User model specs (if any) may no longer exercise it. Add specs for the domain restriction branches.

findings.title: Blocked-email validation only runs when email_changed?, so existing users changing other attributes bypass the blocklist, and email changes are not checked against BlockedEmail
findings.body: `validates :email, email: true, if: :email_changed?` means the custom EmailValidator (which includes the BlockedEmail.should_block? check) only runs when the email attribute has changed. This is intentional for the signup path, but it means: (1) any code path that creates or saves a User with an email that matches a BlockedEmail entry but where email_changed? is false (e.g. an admin editing a user, or a user whose email was set before the blocklist entry was added and who re-saves) will not be blocked; (2) more critically, the change_email flow in UsersController (users_controller.rb:265-286) creates an EmailToken for a new email but never validates the new email against BlockedEmail — a blocked user can change their email to another blocked address via the preferences flow, because EmailToken creation does not run User email validation. The blocklist must also be enforced in the change_email path (and ideally in EmailToken creation), not only on User save with email_changed?.

findings.body: The file ends without a trailing newline (the diff shows '\ No newline at end of file'). This is a minor style issue but can cause problems with some tools and diffs.
